newsitem.title: JAPAN: China sees better atmosphere before WTO talks.
newsitem.headline: China sees better atmosphere before WTO talks.

text.p: A senior Chinese official on Thursday painted a somewhat rosier picture of the potential for progress towards Beijing's joining the World Trade Organisation but said China would "say no" if conditions were set too high.

"There used to be too much emphasis on the aspect that China needs the WTO, so the contracting parties could make any kind of request, which were sometimes not realistic and sometimes beyond the mandate of the WTO," Chinese Vice Trade Minister Long Yongtu said.

"Now, I think the discussions have come to a more balanced view, that China's WTO membership also benefits other contracting parties and is especially important for strengthening the multilateral trade system," he said.

Long was attending a seminar with U.S., European, Japanese and WTO officials as well as businessmen and academics on the issue of China's entry into the world trade body. The seminar comes ahead of negotiations in Geneva in early November.

U.S. and Chinese officials have been at odds for months over the terms for China's entry into the WTO. Beijing has been seeking admission under the more lenient standards set for developing nations, while Washington wants China to meet stricter standards which take its huge economy into account.
Long said there was no timetable for China's entry into the WTO, and reiterated that Beijing would reject any conditions it considered too strict.

"China has not changed its attitude toward its membership in the WTO. The problem is, if members set the threshold of conditions too high, then China cannot afford it. We have to say 'no'. That's a matter of principle," he said.
Some Chinese officials worry that opening the market too quickly would do too much damage to China's loss-making state firms and protected industrial sectors.

WTO Deputy Director General Kim Chul-su said there was agreement that China's WTO membership would benefit the global trade system, but crafting a solution that balanced China's economic needs with the demands of world trade rules was the crux of future talks.

"I think the basic question is how we strike a balance between the needs of the Chinese economy, which is evolving, on the one hand, and honouring the terms and rules of the multilateral trading system," Kim said.
"Since I believe the issues are quite clear now, I hope flexibility and political will on both sides will be forthcoming to see real progress in the negotiations," he said.

A Japanese foreign ministry official told reporters that all seminar participants agreed on the desirability of China joining the WTO. "For investors, it would mean predictability and stability," he said.
Some seminar participants suggested that once the U.S. presidential election was over, momentum toward an agreement on China's accension to the WTO could -- and should -- pick up.

"There should be a compromise that doesn't compromise the credibility of the rules...but in the overall politics of the thing gives it a pragmatic push," said Wendy Dobson, a professor at the University of Toronto.
"Post-election in the U.S. would be a good time for leaders to take a pragmatic and political look at this," she said.
